source.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of EEG Foundation Models via Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: W. Lehn-Schiøler; Magnus Ruud Kjær; Rahul Thapa; Magnus Guldberg Pedersen; A. Storgaard; N. Williams; Radu Gatej; T. Lehn-Schiøler; A. Brink-Kjær; S. Puthusserypady; S. Beniczky; James Zou; Lars Kai Hansen

record.tranche_reason: The study tests SAE features as intervention handles and reports both selective steering and entangled or non-selective failures. It explicitly cautions that observational separability does not guarantee selective intervention, refining the claim that dictionary features are canonical units.
record.gate_note: The paper uses superposition as motivation and applies SAEs to EEG foundation models. It does not test toy-model superposition geometry, neuron-capacity competition, or LLM representations. Expansion-factor results used to choose operating points are hyperparameter-selection outcomes, not rows. Quantitative steering curves are in figures without values in the text; only explicitly described outcomes are recorded.
record.test_reason: The study applies TopK SAEs to three finetuned EEG transformers as an interpretability tool. It reports reconstruction fidelity, a taxonomy of concept-enriched features, and the selectivity of concept steering, all from its own pipeline. None of these bear on a claim version. V1–V3 concern toy networks and neuron capacity, which are not studied. V4 concerns LLMs, and these are EEG encoders. V5 concerns whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units. The steering results instead clamp the top-n concept-aligned features as a group to a target centroid. They measure how entangled clinical concepts are in the encoder, not whether individual dictionary features are the model's canonical units. No stability across seeds or datasets, and no completeness, is tested. The reader's T5 classification of V5 is therefore not adopted.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. The authors present a model-agnostic SAE, concept-steering and spectral-decoding framework for auditing EEG foundation models. It separates selectively steerable, entangled (wrecking-ball) and weakly encoded clinical concepts, and grounds interventions in spectral signatures. They also caution that separability does not guarantee selectivity.
record.recipe_differences: The study applies layer-wise TopK SAEs and clinical-concept steering to finetuned EEG transformers; it does not reproduce toy-model feature geometry or the original toy-network experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by encoder, layer, and target concept: selective steering is reported for some settings, while other settings are entangled or weakly encoded.

fits_no_version.finding: TopK-SAE reconstructions preserve the normal/abnormal classifier AUROC within 0.017 across all layers of three EEG encoders.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In finetuned EEG transformers, TopK-SAE reconstructions preserve task-relevant classification performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Clamping concept-aligned SAE features shows mixed results. Some encoder/layer/concept cells are selectively steerable (SleepFM abnormality and age; LaBraM ASM). Others are encoded but not steerable (REVE abnormality) or show wrecking-ball collapse, with excess selectivity ≈0 (SleepFM L1 psychiatric medication; LaBraM L4 age). The authors state that observational separability does not guarantee interventional selectivity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Observationally separable SAE concept features need not provide selective causal intervention handles; selectivity varies by encoder, layer and concept.

record.problems: Steering outcomes are largely described qualitatively in the text, while the curves and many numerical values appear only in figures. The authors also note that their investigator-defined concepts bound the audit, and that the spectral decoder cannot recover phase or exact time-domain morphology.
record.rows_left_out: The text reports expansion-factor selections and steering-curve summaries mainly through figures; numerical figure-only values were not extracted. The n = 104 steering spectrum is shown in Figure 6 but not described with an explicit textual outcome, so it was omitted.

untested.parts: All parts: toy networks, sparsity-dependent transition, near-orthogonal geometry.
All parts: capacity competition and dedicated versus shared dimensions.
All parts: non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
All parts. The models are EEG transformers, not LLMs.
Completeness, stability across seeds or datasets, and canonicity of SAE features. Steering acts on groups of features and measures concept entanglement instead.

record.verdict_notes: The separable/entangled/dead taxonomy fractions across layers and expansion factors (Fig. 3) are figure-only and were used to choose operating points. They are not a test of any version. Superposition is cited only as motivation (ref. [8], the original source). Sex being weakly encoded in all encoders serves as the authors' implicit negative control.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, feature sparsity and importance sweeps, overlapping near-orthogonal directions, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity arises from limited capacity, and whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while others share.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
The study concerns EEG foundation models, not LLMs, and does not test whether LLM features are distributed across neurons or recovered by SAEs.
The study tests SAE features as concept-steering handles, but not whether they are complete, stable across runs or datasets, or canonical units of the model representation.
Whether represented features are intrinsically one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Concept steering across the reported EEG model/layer/concept settings
reader_labels.reason: Some SAE features support selective steering, but the paper reports non-steerable abnormality in representative REVE layers and entangled wrecking-ball cases; separability does not guarantee selectivity (R4–R8).
